prompt.context: Our client is a coffin maker in the Eastern European country of Maldovia. He has seen substantial change in his market in recent years and is contemplating the future of his business. Up until now, he has been in the business of building high-quality, hand-crafted coffins largely by hand with a skilled labor force. Recently, however, he has become aware of technology that would allow him to build machine-made coffins with much less labor.
prompt.question: Should he invest in this new technology, and should he even remain in the coffin business in the first place? What strategic alternatives should the owner consider?

clarifying_info.q: What is the population of Maldovia?
What is the population growth rate?

clarifying_info.a: Assume a flat distribution — the same number of people at all ages
75% of deaths are buried in coffins

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's market share?
clarifying_info.a: Maldovian Coffins has a 10% market share and a relative market share of about 1 (relative market share is the ratio of the company's market share to that of its nearest competitor)

clarifying_info.q: What are the trends, regulation, or other exogenous factors in the market?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the market is expected to continue as it currently is

clarifying_info.q: What is the current price and cost structure?
clarifying_info.a: Coffins are priced at $5,000 for a hand-made coffin. Material accounts for 10% of direct cost; labor accounts for 90%. COGS is $4,800 per coffin. Fixed costs are $700,000 per year. All assets are fully depreciated; ignore taxes.

clarifying_info.q: How much does the new technology cost and what does it change?
clarifying_info.a: Investing in the new technology will cost $1M. Material costs remain the same, but labor costs will be reduced by 50%.
The technology is currently offered for sale by a machine tool company that holds the patent. They are not offering exclusivity — they will sell to competitors as well.

clarifying_info.q: Have competitors acquired or are they planning to acquire this technology?
clarifying_info.a: It is not known whether competitors have acquired or are planning to acquire this technology.

clarifying_info.q: How do customers perceive machine-made vs. hand-made coffins?
clarifying_info.a: The quality perceived by the customer is the same or better. Customers are believed to be indifferent between the quality and appearance of a hand-made and a machine-made coffin.

clarifying_info.q: What assets does the company own?
clarifying_info.a: Since the firm has been building coffins by hand, the fixed assets are essentially only land and improvements. The company owns these assets outright.

clarifying_info.q: What is the value of the land and improvements?
clarifying_info.a: Book value of land: $20,000. Book value of improvements: $80,000. The property has been owned for 48 years. Average real estate appreciation is 6% per year.

framework: Strategic decision tree: (1) Continue operating — either without new technology or by investing in new technology; (2) Exit the business — either sell to a third party or liquidate assets
Market analysis: industry trends (declining profitability, technology disruption), competition (market share, relative market share), total market size
Client profile: competitive advantages (skilled labor), profitability (margins, direction), total assets (land, equipment, buildings)
Valuation comparison: value of business as a going concern (with and without technology) vs. value of liquidated assets

questions.prompt: Calculate the market size — how many coffins are purchased per year in Maldovia?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that 1/75th of the population dies each year (flat age distribution, 75-year life expectancy), then apply the 75% burial rate. Strong answer arrives at 40,000 coffins/year cleanly.

math.setup: Population 4,000,000; life expectancy 75 years; flat age distribution means 1/75 die per year; 75% are buried in coffins

questions.prompt: Calculate the current value of the business (without new technology).
questions.guidance: Candidate should build up unit economics, compute annual profit, then value as a perpetuity at 10% discount rate. Should arrive at $1M.

math.setup: Price $5,000; COGS $4,800 (labor 90% = $4,320, material 10% = $480); contribution margin $200; units sold = 40,000 × 10% = 4,000; fixed costs $700,000/year; discount rate 10%

questions.prompt: What would happen if competitors also adopt the new technology? How would pricing change, and what is the value of the business WITH the new technology?
questions.guidance: Key insight: the technology is non-proprietary, so competitors will likely adopt it, driving down industry costs and prices. The interviewer provides the assumption that gross margin stays at 4%. Candidate should recalculate new price, new unit economics, and new value — then recognize the investment destroys value.

math.setup: Current gross margin = $200/$5,000 = 4%. With new technology: labor cost = $4,320 × 50% = $2,160; material cost = $480; new COGS = $2,640. New price at 4% gross margin = $2,640 / (1 − 0.04) = $2,750. Units and market share unchanged at 4,000 units.
math.answer: Value with new technology = −$3,600,000; investing in the technology destroys value

questions.prompt: If the business is shut down and assets liquidated, what is the value of the real estate?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm at least 3 methods to value the land before being given data (comparables sale price; discounted rental cash flows; apply appreciation rate to book value). Then apply the rule of 72 to compute current value. Final comparison: liquidation value ($1.6M) > going-concern value ($1M), so liquidating is superior.

math.setup: Book value of land + improvements = $20,000 + $80,000 = $100,000. Held for 48 years. Average appreciation = 6%/year. Rule of 72: doubles every 72/6 = 12 years. 48 years = 4 doubling periods.

brainstorming.prompt: How would you determine the value of real estate you have never appraised before?

categories.name: Market comparables
ideas: Look for comparable real estate transactions in the area and determine recent selling prices
Identify comparable commercial real estate and determine rent per square foot, then discount the resulting cash flows

categories.name: Historical appreciation
ideas: Determine the historical rate of real estate appreciation in the area and apply it to the book value of current land and improvements

categories.name: Income approach
ideas: Estimate potential rental income from the property and apply a cap rate to derive value

categories.name: Replacement cost
ideas: Estimate the cost to replace the land improvements at current construction prices

recommendation: The client should liquidate the business and sell its assets rather than continuing to operate or investing in the new machine-making technology
The real estate value ($1.6M) exceeds the going-concern value ($1M), making liquidation the value-maximizing choice
Investing in the new technology would destroy approximately $3.6M in value given the non-proprietary nature of the technology and resulting competitive price erosion
risks: If competitors do not adopt the new technology, the price reduction assumption does not hold and the client may retain current profitability — but the $1M going-concern value still falls short of the $1.6M liquidation value
Introduction of new technology to the market by any competitor may erode industry margins, making the $1M going-concern value untenable even without the client's own investment
Real estate valuation using the rule of 72 is an approximation; a professional appraisal should confirm the $1.6M estimate
next_steps: Obtain a professional real estate appraisal to confirm liquidation value
Explore sale of the going concern to a strategic buyer who may pay a premium above liquidation value
Assess employee severance obligations and any regulatory requirements for business closure in Maldovia
